name: theworldofai.org: AI Laws by State tracker and analysis
title: theworldofai.org: AI Laws by State tracker and analysis
answer: theworldofai.org's AI Laws page is a state-by-state tracker and comparison of US artificial intelligence legislation. It says it tracks 6,000 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan and linked to official bill pages. Its most useful finding is that no two states wrote the same law, yet recurring duties appear: disclose AI use, keep a qualified person in decisions about health, employment, benefits or education, run a crisis protocol for conversational products, keep records, and expect attorneys general to enforce.

sections.body: theworldofai.org publishes this AI Laws page. It is a tracker and analysis of US state artificial intelligence legislation, not a single bill or agency document. The text says it covers 6,000 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database and linked to each bill's official page. It also presents a comparison of 101 enrolled measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026. The page says every page is rebuilt daily from primary sources and carries the date it was last verified. It is free to read, cite and query. The same text also promotes books by Stephen R. Jordan and services from SRJ Consulting & Services.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The source says US AI legislation is written state by state, and the page tracks all of it. It reports 6,000 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan and linked to official pages. From enrolled text of passed measures, it compared 101 measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026. It says no two states wrote the same law, but the same choices recur. Only Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149 passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors. Every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. Where stakes are personal, the rule is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider. Insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone. AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician. It cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation. New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law. The attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively. Several states declare a violation an unfair or deceptive trade practice under consumer protection law. The source advises telling people when they deal with AI, keeping a qualified person in decisions about health, employment, benefits or education, having a crisis protocol and knowing user age for conversational products, and keeping records.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states 6,000 AI bills tracked across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan. It states 101 measures across 27 states were compared, reviewed on September 18, 2026. It states no two states wrote the same law. It states only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. It states no state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law. It states the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation an unfair or deceptive trade practice under consumer protection law. It states a private right to sue is the exception, mainly where one identifiable person is harmed. It states New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. It states AI may assist but may not be the only decider where stakes are personal.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Government can use this source to see how state legislatures are writing AI rules that touch government agencies, benefit decisions, classrooms and enforcement. It shows that the attorney general is the main enforcer in the larger laws, that no new agency was created in this set, and that New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. It also shows a patchwork of sector-specific measures, which matters for procurement, compliance and oversight across states. The source links to official bill pages, so it can serve as a starting point for tracking specific state AI laws, though it is a tracker and comparison rather than legal advice.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Government

sections.body: The source text focuses on state AI legislation and does not describe federal AI legislation. It is a commercial page from theworldofai.org and includes promotions for books by Stephen R. Jordan and services from SRJ Consulting & Services. It gives a comparison reviewed on September 18, 2026, and says pages are rebuilt daily, but it does not give full bill text, only links. It does not cover local ordinances, law outside the United States, implementation outcomes or court results beyond mentioning a lawsuit tracker elsewhere on the site. It is not legal advice.
